sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**VohuManah** (*vohumanah*) — Good Mind, Cattle · Good thought — belongs to the Zoroastrian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Good Mind, Cattle". The name means "Good thought".

**VohuManah** is good mind, cattle. The name means "Good thought" and belongs to the zoroastrian tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **VohuManah** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/vohumanah/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *vohumanah* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Avestan as **𐬬𐬊𐬵𐬎 𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵**. Etymologically it means "Good thought".

The ASCII form *vohumanah* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **VohuManah** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2.

sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/vohumanah/** — Restored scholarly form.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **vohumanah** — The canonical restored form VohuManah.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: Say "vohumanah" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "VohuManah".

The ASCII form "vohumanah" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "VohuManah" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

The pronunciation given above reconstructs the sound world in which VohuManah was invoked. Modern speakers should not expect exact identity with ancient phonology; the reconstruction is a scholarly compass, not a performance prescription. The restoration VohuManah keeps the prosodic information visible even when the name is typed in plain ASCII.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in Avestan as **𐬬𐬊𐬵𐬎 𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵**.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Vohu Manah*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Vohu Manah is one of the Amesha Spentas praised in the Gathas.
- The final -h in Vohu and Manah represents Avestan h (𐬵).
- The vowel o in Vohu is written with the Avestan letter o (𐬊).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The stories of VohuManah place good mind, cattle at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

VohuManah appears in zoroastrian tradition as good mind, cattle. The name's meaning, "Good thought", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved VohuManah in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of VohuManah survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration VohuManah gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Within the Zoroastrian tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[ahriman|Ahriman]], [[ahuramazda|AhuraMazdā]], [[ameretat|Amərətāt]], [[anahita|Anāhitā]], [[asa|Aša]], and [[ashavahista|Ašavahišta]].

Cross-cultural identifications are rarely one-to-one. VohuManah may be likened to figures in neighboring traditions without being identical to them. The PuniCodex crosslink index records these resonances as relationships, not equations. The restored form VohuManah makes such comparisons possible across language boundaries.

sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
VohuManah remains a touchstone for understanding zoroastrian religion, art, and identity.

The modern afterlife of VohuManah includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning for a new audience. The PuniCodex temple participates in that afterlife by ensuring that the restored name VohuManah remains findable and citable.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to VohuManah with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Zoroastrian name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming 𐬬𐬊𐬵𐬎 𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵, sanctuary or cult remains tied to good mind and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

sections.label: The Gathas
sections.body:
The Gāthās, the hymns attributed to Zarathuštra, are the oldest stratum of Zoroastrian scripture. VohuManah appears in the later Avestan and Middle Persian reception rather than the Gāthās themselves, but the ethical dualism of the hymns shapes the figure's role as good mind.

The restoration VohuManah follows Avestan scholarly convention.

sections.label: The Avesta
sections.body:
The Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrianism, preserves liturgical and mythological traditions in Old and Young Avestan. VohuManah is embedded in hymns, rituals, and cosmological lists that define the Zoroastrian pantheon.

The restored form VohuManah carries the diacritic detail of Avestan scholarship.

sections.label: Middle Persian & Sasanian Texts
sections.body:
Middle Persian (Pahlavi) Zoroastrian texts — the Bundahišn, Dēnkard, and Zand commentaries — transmit VohuManah into the Sasanian and post-Sasanian periods. These sources render the name in the Pahlavi script and interpret its place in the cosmic order.

The Unicode restoration VohuManah bridges Avestan and Pahlavi forms.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
To contemplate VohuManah is to hold the idea of good Mind, Cattle in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "Good thought" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as good Mind, Cattle · Good thought.

Sit with the restored form — VohuManah — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *vohumanah* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.
